questions.question: When should you use a channel instead of a Mutex in Go?
questions.title: Channels versus Mutexes
questions.direct_answer: Use a Mutex when several goroutines need short, synchronous access to shared in-memory state or a compound invariant. Use a channel when communication, ownership transfer, work delivery, backpressure, or cancellation is the central relationship. Neither is universally more idiomatic: choose the primitive that expresses the state owner and lifecycle clearly, and do not turn a simple locked counter into an unnecessary goroutine protocol.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses from ownership and coordination needs rather than repeating a slogan.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Mutex fits short access to shared state and invariants.
Channels fit communication, ownership transfer, and workflow coordination.
A channel can give mutable state one goroutine owner.
A Mutex avoids a separate goroutine lifecycle for simple shared state.
Choose from the data flow and measure contention when it matters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Channels and Mutexes both help build correct concurrent programs, but they express different relationships. A Mutex says several goroutines share this state and must enter its critical section one at a time. A channel says goroutines communicate by sending values or lifecycle events.

I prefer a Mutex for a small cache, counter with related fields, or map that many request handlers read and update synchronously. The protected operation can return directly, and there is no separate owner goroutine, queue capacity, send path, or shutdown protocol to manage.

I prefer a channel when work already forms a stream, a producer must apply backpressure, a result needs delivery, or ownership of mutable state can stay in one goroutine. For example, workers can send integer deltas to one counter goroutine; only that owner changes the total, so the total itself needs no lock.

Channels are not automatic race prevention. Sending a pointer and then mutating the pointed value from both sides still shares memory. Mutexes are not automatically simpler if callers need cancellation while waiting for an entire workflow. The surrounding ownership contract decides safety.

I start by asking who owns the data and whether the operation is state access or communication. A short shared-memory transition suggests a Mutex; a lifecycle or handoff suggests a channel. I then keep the chosen API narrow and measure only if contention or throughput becomes a demonstrated problem.

sections.title: Concept guide · Channels versus Mutexes
sections.content: Mutex keeps shared ownership and serializes access. Channel can move values or commands to a single owner and naturally represents waiting between stages. Both require explicit lifetime and access rules; the better model is the one readers can verify locally.

sections.title: Compare the complete cost of each model
sections.content:
A locked map has one object and one synchronization boundary. Methods acquire the guard, perform a bounded operation, and return. This is direct and type-safe for request handlers that need immediate lookup or update. Contention depends on how often and how long callers hold the lock.

A channel-owner design adds a goroutine and message protocol. Requests may include a reply channel when callers need results. Capacity decides whether producers block, queue, or use an explicit drop policy. Shutdown decides when senders stop and who closes each channel. Those costs are worthwhile when they match an existing workflow, not merely to avoid the word shared.

Ownership must include referenced data. Sending a slice header transfers only a descriptor; its backing array can remain aliased elsewhere. A safe handoff means the sender stops mutating the transferred object, or it sends an immutable copy. Communication establishes ordering but does not erase aliases.

The counter-owner example receives deltas until its input closes, then sends one result. The goroutine is the only writer, and channel close defines completion. For a method that needs the current total during operation, the protocol would need query messages or another safe snapshot path, making a Mutex potentially simpler.

Effective Go's communication slogan is a design direction, not a ban on locks. The sync package explicitly supplies low-level primitives, and standard Go code uses them where appropriate. Prefer the model that makes ownership, blocking, and shutdown visible; profile before replacing a clear solution with more elaborate synchronization.

sections.title: Two valid ownership models
sections.content:
| Question | Mutex model | Channel model |
|---|---|---|
| Who owns state? | Several callers under one guard | Usually one receiving goroutine |
| Natural operation | Synchronous read or update | Message, handoff, or workflow event |
| Backpressure | Lock contention | Send blocks or queue policy applies |
| Extra lifecycle | Lock identity | Goroutine and channel shutdown |
| Typical example | Shared cache | Worker queue or pipeline |

questions.question: How do you choose among Mutex, RWMutex, and sync/atomic?
questions.title: Mutex, RWMutex, and atomic operations
questions.direct_answer: Use Mutex as the clear default for compound state. Consider RWMutex only for measured read-heavy contention where concurrent readers materially help and writes remain manageable. Use typed sync/atomic operations for a small independent value whose complete state transition is representable atomically. Atomics do not make several fields one transaction, and a more complicated primitive should earn its cost through a real access pattern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner matches the primitive to invariant size and measured contention.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Mutex is the simple default for compound state.
RWMutex permits concurrent readers but excludes writers.
Choose RWMutex only after the read-heavy pattern matters in measurement.
Typed atomics fit independent counters, flags, or pointers.
Several atomic fields do not become one atomic invariant.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`sync.Mutex` is my default for shared mutable state because one Lock/Unlock protocol is easy to review and can protect several fields as one invariant. Its zero value works immediately, and the critical section can contain a complete check and update.

`sync.RWMutex` adds read locks. Several goroutines may hold `RLock` concurrently, while a writer using `Lock` excludes readers and other writers. That can help a genuinely read-heavy workload with enough lock contention, but bookkeeping and longer reader occupancy can make it no faster or even worse.

Typed values in `sync/atomic`, such as `atomic.Int64`, provide indivisible operations on one value. They are a good fit for an independent request count or published pointer when the required transitions are fully expressed by Load, Store, Add, Swap, or compare-and-swap.

For example, a Stats type can increment a total request metric atomically while using one Mutex to update the related pair `lastUser` and `lastPath`. Making those two fields separate atomics would not give readers one coherent pair.

I choose correctness from the invariant first. Then I benchmark or profile if ordinary Mutex contention matters. RWMutex and atomics are specialized tools, not automatic upgrades. A primitive is appropriate when its API exactly represents every permitted access and leaves the resulting ownership rule easier—not harder—to prove. I keep the measurement and race-enabled tests so a later change can be compared safely.

sections.title: Invariant size comes before read/write ratio
sections.content: Atomic operations cover one small state machine. Locks cover a critical section that may span several values. RWMutex changes which lock holders may overlap. Identify the state transition first, then examine contention and access frequency.

sections.title: Avoid optimizing away the synchronization contract
sections.content:
A Mutex serializes all holders, which is often inexpensive when the protected operation is short. It provides one straightforward place to preserve relationships among fields. Starting with it keeps benchmarks honest because any later change can be compared against a correct baseline.

RWMutex separates read and write acquisition. Concurrent readers can proceed together, but writers need exclusive access, and a pending writer affects new readers according to the lock's starvation-avoidance behavior. Recursive read locking and lock upgrades are not supported patterns. Long reads can still delay mutation.

Atomics avoid a conventional critical section for supported operations. Go's atomic operations provide sequentially consistent ordering, but they do not compose automatically. Reading atomic field A and then field B can observe values from different logical updates unless the design uses a versioning protocol or a single atomically published immutable object.

The Stats example makes that boundary visible. Request count has no relationship to a particular last-request pair, so Add and Load can be atomic. User and path must describe the same request, so one Mutex protects their update and snapshot together. Different primitives coexist because the invariants are different.

Measure before reaching for RWMutex or a custom atomic protocol. Use the mutex and blocking profiles and representative benchmarks. If lock contention is not a meaningful share of time, extra states increase maintenance risk without user benefit. Correct, readable synchronization is a performance feature because it makes future optimization measurable.

sections.title: Match primitive to state shape
sections.content:
| Primitive | Protects best | Concurrent access | Main caution |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Mutex` | Compound invariant | One holder | Keep section bounded |
| `RWMutex` | Measured read-heavy state | Many readers or one writer | Not automatically faster |
| Typed atomic | One independent word/state machine | Atomic operations | Does not compose fields |

sections.title: Use different primitives for different invariants

questions.question: What is the difference between WaitGroup, channels, and context cancellation?
questions.title: Completion, communication, and cancellation
questions.direct_answer: WaitGroup answers whether a set of tasks has finished. Channels transfer values or lifecycle signals and can apply backpressure. Context propagates cancellation, deadlines, and request-scoped information through an API call tree. They often work together: workers watch Context, send results on a channel, and a WaitGroup lets a coordinator close that result channel only after every sender has returned.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner assigns completion, result transport, and cancellation to the correct tools.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: WaitGroup tracks completion; it carries no result or cancellation.
Channels carry values, readiness, backpressure, or simple signals.
Context propagates cancellation and deadlines through API boundaries.
The sender side owns closure of a result channel.
These tools compose because they answer different questions.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
WaitGroup, channels, and Context are not competing versions of one feature. A WaitGroup represents task completion. A channel represents communication or a lifecycle event. Context represents a propagated request lifetime with cancellation, deadlines, and limited request-scoped values.

WaitGroup is useful when a coordinator must know all workers have returned. It does not transport their values and calling Wait does not ask them to stop. A results channel can carry values or errors, while its capacity and sends define backpressure.

Context lets a caller cancel a tree of operations. Workers select on `ctx.Done()` while attempting blocking work and normally return `ctx.Err()` when canceled. CancelFunc requests that stop but does not wait for it, so completion tracking remains separate.

For example, two workers read jobs, compute squares, and send results. They also watch Context. A WaitGroup tracks both workers, and a small closer goroutine waits before closing results. The consumer can safely range over results because no sender remains after closure.

I use each primitive for one sentence: Context says stop, channels say here is data, and WaitGroup says all senders are finished. Keeping those responsibilities separate prevents common errors such as closing a result channel while workers still send or assuming cancellation has already completed cleanup. Tests should cancel early as well as finish normally and prove every worker and result channel reaches its promised final state.

sections.title: Three questions need three signals
sections.content: A worker system needs to know when to stop, how to deliver output, and when every sender is gone. Context, result channels, and WaitGroup answer those questions independently, which lets their ownership rules remain visible.

sections.title: Assemble a worker lifecycle without overloaded signals
sections.content:
Jobs and results are data streams. The coordinator closes jobs when no more work will arrive. Workers receive until that close or cancellation. Results remain open while any worker can send, so workers themselves cannot independently decide when the shared output is finished.

WaitGroup counts those possible senders. Start each worker through Go or register it before launch. Another goroutine calls Wait and closes results after the count reaches zero. That close is safe because the completion guarantee proves no worker can execute a later send.

Context adds early termination. A worker includes `ctx.Done()` in selects around blocking receive or send operations. If a client cancels, the worker returns instead of remaining stuck behind an abandoned consumer. The creator calls CancelFunc to release resources but still waits or drains results according to the API contract.

Errors require a design choice. They may travel as part of a result value, through a buffered first-error channel, or through a higher-level error group that also cancels siblings. WaitGroup alone cannot surface them, and Context's Err reports why the context ended rather than every task's domain failure.

The example completes normally but already has cancellation paths at both blocking boundaries. Its result closer waits for all workers, making range termination trustworthy. This pattern scales because every close has one owner and every synchronization primitive communicates only the fact it is designed to represent.

sections.title: Different signals across one worker pool
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Context: stop request] --> W1[Worker 1]
  C --> W2[Worker 2]
  J[Jobs channel: input] --> W1
  J --> W2
  W1 --> R[Results channel: output]
  W2 --> R
  W1 --> G[WaitGroup: completion]
  W2 --> G
  G -->|all returned| X[Close results]
```
